fields.expected:
Most of my AI work has been in retrieval, agents, and evaluation. In Gloria I built the retrieval layer with OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph to represent memories and relationships, plus a conversation state machine that moved interactions through prompting, drafting, refinement, and finalization. At Summer Atlantic Capital I work on temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and an LLM explanation layer built on retrieval-augmented generation, all served through a versioned FastAPI microservice.

On the agent side, I built a Playwright browser agent in TypeScript and Node where OpenAI is called only at narrow call sites, with SQLite as the single source of truth and Zod validation, because letting a model drive arbitrary browser state is how you accidentally submit a real application. In tSearch I built rubric-driven LLM judges that evaluate separate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize an evidence-cited assessment.

I also have model training experience: XGBoost with SHAP on roughly 10 million survey records, and a PyTorch CNN for facial-landmark prediction at about 95% PCK. From my Intelehealth work evaluating LLM outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, I care about evaluation as much as generation.

Most of my AI work has been in retrieval, agents, and evaluation. In Gloria I built the retrieval layer with OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph to represent memories and relationships, plus a conversation state machine that moved interactions through prompting, drafting, refinement, and finalization. At Summer Atlantic Capital I work on temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and an LLM explanation layer built on retrieval-augmented generation, all served through a versioned FastAPI microservice.

On the agent side, I built a Playwright browser agent in TypeScript and Node where OpenAI is called only at narrow call sites, with SQLite as the single source of truth and Zod validation, because letting a model drive arbitrary browser state is how you accidentally submit a real application. In tSearch I built rubric-driven LLM judges that evaluate separate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize an evidence-cited assessment.

I also have model training experience: XGBoost with SHAP on roughly 10 million survey records, and a PyTorch CNN for facial-landmark prediction at about 95% PCK. From my Intelehealth work evaluating LLM outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, I care about evaluation as much as generation.

fields.expected: Notion describes itself as a workspace where teams and agents think together, and the agent half of that is the problem I have spent the most time on. I built a local Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine, SQLite is the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being autofilled and always generate a human-review item. I also built a validation ladder so a capability is not called working just because it passed against a local fixture. That work, plus designing an evaluation framework for LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case benchmark at Intelehealth, made me care about a specific question: when an agent acts inside someone's real workspace, how do you decide what it is allowed to do and how do you know its output should be trusted. That is the part I would want to work on at Notion, on a product people actually use every day rather than a demo.
